goals.goal: rust rustc error[E0502]: cannot borrow `*a` as mutable because `a` is also borrowed as immutable - what does it mean and how do I fix it?

nuggets.text: E0502 occurs when a variable already borrowed with one mutability (mutable or immutable) is borrowed again with a different mutability.
The documented example error is 'cannot borrow `*a` as mutable because `a` is also borrowed as immutable'.
The fix is to ensure there are no other live references to the variable before accessing it with a different mutability.
In the documented fix, the mutable use (bar(a)) is moved before the immutable borrow (let y = &a), so the borrows do not overlap.
The E0502 page points to the References & Borrowing section of the Rust Book for more on ownership.

goals.goal: rustc error[E0382]: borrow of moved value / use of moved value - what causes it and what are the ways to fix it?

nuggets.text: E0382 means a variable was used after its contents have been moved elsewhere.
A value of a type not marked Copy is moved on assignment (let y = x), so the original variable can no longer be used.
One fix is to pass a reference (&) instead of moving the value, e.g. calculate_length(&s1); a mutable reference uses &mut.
Another fix is to duplicate the value by calling .clone() on a type that implements Clone, or by adding #[derive(Clone)] to your own type.
Types whose members are all Copy can be marked #[derive(Copy, Clone)] so assignment copies instead of moving.
If mutable shared ownership is truly required, use Rc together with RefCell (RefCell does runtime borrow checking).

goals.goal: git says 'fatal: refusing to merge unrelated histories' when I run git pull or git merge. What does it mean and how do I get past it?

nuggets.text: By default, git merge refuses to merge histories that do not share a common ancestor.
The override is the --allow-unrelated-histories option of git merge, meant for merging two projects that started their lives independently.
Git docs say no configuration variable to enable --allow-unrelated-histories by default exists or will be added, because this is a very rare occasion.
git pull also accepts --allow-unrelated-histories, which is only useful when merging (not rebasing).

goals.goal: Node.js Error [ERR_REQUIRE_ESM]: require() of ES Module not supported - what does this error mean and does it still happen on current Node versions?

nuggets.text: ERR_REQUIRE_ESM means an attempt was made to require() an ES Module.
ERR_REQUIRE_ESM is deprecated because require() now supports loading synchronous ES modules.
require(esm) no longer needs the --experimental-require-module flag as of v23.0.0, v22.12.0 and v20.19.0.
require() can only load an ES module that is fully synchronous, i.e. contains no top-level await.
A file qualifies as ESM for require() if it has a .mjs extension, or is a .js file whose closest package.json has "type": "module".
If the required ES module contains top-level await, require() throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE instead.

goals.goal: PostgreSQL ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint, SQLSTATE 23505 - what does this code mean and how can I avoid the error on insert?

nuggets.text: SQLSTATE 23505 has the condition name unique_violation.
23505 belongs to SQLSTATE Class 23, Integrity Constraint Violation (alongside not_null_violation 23502, foreign_key_violation 23503 and check_violation 23514).
PostgreSQL error codes are five-character SQLSTATE codes, and applications should usually test the code rather than the localized message text.
For a unique_violation the server reports the name of the unique constraint in a separate error field.
INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING simply skips inserting a conflicting row, while ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE updates the existing conflicting row.

goals.goal: I'm getting HTTP 429 Too Many Requests from an API. What does 429 mean and how should my client respond?

nuggets.text: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests indicates the client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.
This mechanism of asking the client to slow down is commonly called rate limiting.
A 429 response may include a Retry-After header indicating how long the client should wait before making the request again.
Rate-limiting restrictions are typically based on the client's IP, but can be per user or per authorized application.
The 429 status code is defined in RFC 6585, section 4.

goals.goal: Python RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded - what triggers it and can I raise the limit?

nuggets.text: RecursionError is raised when the interpreter detects that the maximum recursion depth is exceeded.
RecursionError derives from RuntimeError and was added in Python 3.5; previously a plain RuntimeError was raised.
sys.getrecursionlimit() returns the current maximum depth of the Python interpreter stack.
sys.setrecursionlimit(limit) sets the maximum depth; the limit exists to prevent infinite recursion from overflowing the C stack and crashing Python.
Setting the limit too high can crash the interpreter, and the highest possible limit is platform-dependent.
sys.setrecursionlimit raises RecursionError if the new limit is too low at the current recursion depth.

goals.goal: Docker prints 'WARNING: Error loading config file: /home/user/.docker/config.json - stat /home/user/.docker/config.json: permission denied'. What causes this and how do I fix it?

nuggets.text: The error indicates the permission settings for the ~/.docker/ directory are incorrect, due to having used the sudo command earlier.
One fix is to remove the ~/.docker/ directory; it is recreated automatically but any custom settings are lost.
Another fix is sudo chown "$USER":"$USER" /home/"$USER"/.docker -R to change ownership.
The ownership fix is followed by sudo chmod g+rwx "$HOME/.docker" -R to set permissions.
To run docker without sudo, add your user to the docker group with sudo usermod -aG docker $USER, then log out and back in (or run newgrp docker).
The docker group grants root-level privileges to the user.
